what-is-ai-for-kids:
The explanation matters more than usual here, because a child's first mental model of what these systems are tends to stick, and the two easy explanations are both wrong in ways that cause problems later.

The first wrong model is that it is a person in the computer. The second is that it is a very big search engine that looks up answers. A child holding either will trust it in the wrong places.

The model that holds up

It is a machine that has read an enormous amount of writing and has become very good at guessing what word comes next.

That is not a simplification for children. It is close to what is actually happening, and it explains almost everything a child will notice: why it sounds fluent, why it sometimes states things that are not true with complete confidence, why it can write a poem about a dog on a bicycle, and why it does not know what happened yesterday.

How to say it, by age

Five to seven. "It is a computer that has read millions of books and stories, so it is very good at guessing what to say next. It is not alive and it does not know things the way you know things. Sometimes its guesses are wrong."

At this age the useful part is the last sentence. A child who expects it to be wrong sometimes is in a much better position than one who does not.

Eight to eleven. Add the mechanism. It was shown huge amounts of text and learned which words tend to follow which. It does not look up an answer and it does not check. So it can be fluent and wrong at the same time, which is a combination people are not used to and are bad at spotting.

Also add: it learned from what people wrote, so it picked up their mistakes and their unfairness along with everything else.

Twelve and up. The interesting conversations become available. Why does it have no memory of you between conversations. What does it mean that it has no way to check what it says. Who decided what it should refuse to answer. What is it for, from the point of view of whoever built it.

The demonstration worth doing

Ask it something you know well and can check. A local detail, a family fact, something about your street. Watch it produce a confident, plausible, wrong answer, and let your child see that happen.

One demonstration of confident wrongness does more than any amount of warning, because the warning is abstract and this is not.

What to be careful of in your own framing

Avoid saying it thinks, knows, wants or understands, even casually. Those words build the wrong model quickly and they are hard to unbuild. "It generated", "it produced", "it guessed" are all available and all more accurate.

Equally, avoid dismissing it as useless. Children can tell when an adult is uncomfortable rather than informed, and it ends the conversation.

A child who understands that it guesses, fluently, and cannot check itself has most of what they need. Everything else is built on that.
should-children-use-ai:
Whether is not the useful question, because the answer is already yes for most children over ten and will be yes for the rest. The useful question is what for, and there is a clean line between two kinds of use.

The line

Does the tool support the child's thinking, or replace it?

Everything else follows from that, and it is a line a child can learn to apply themselves, which matters because you will not be in the room.

Supports thinkingReplaces thinking
Explaining something they did not understand in class, a second wayProducing the answer to the question they were set
Asking it to quiz them on what they have revisedAsking it to write the essay
Arguing with it about a position they holdAsking it what position to hold
Asking why their code does not work, after tryingAsking for code before trying
Getting five ideas to react to when stuckGetting five ideas and picking one to submit
Translating a word while reading in another languageTranslating the whole passage instead of reading it

How to tell which one is happening

One question, and it works on any subject: can you explain this to me without the screen.

A child who used it to understand something can. A child who used it to skip something cannot, and both of you will know within thirty seconds. It is not a punishment, it is a check, and it can be a normal part of the household rather than an accusation.

The genuine risks, in order

Confident wrongness. These systems produce fluent, plausible, incorrect statements with no signal that anything is wrong. A child who has not seen this happen will not expect it.

Skipping the difficulty. The struggle in the middle of a hard task is where the learning is. A tool that removes it feels like help and is not, and the cost is invisible for a long time.

Outsourcing judgement. The worry is less that a child cheats and more that they stop forming their own view because a fluent one is always available.

Data. What they type is sent somewhere. Most children need telling that at least once.

What is genuinely good about it

Worth saying, because a purely negative framing is both inaccurate and ends the conversation. It is a patient explainer that never sighs, which matters enormously for a child who is embarrassed to ask again. It will explain the same thing five different ways. It is a tireless quizzer. And for a child who finds writing physically hard, it removes a barrier that has nothing to do with their thinking.

Where it should stay out

Anything that is practice rather than production. Early reading and writing, arithmetic while it is being learned, and the first draft of anything they are meant to be learning to draft. The point of those is the doing.

Your child is not competing with these systems. What is worth building is the thing that decides when to use one, which is judgement, and judgement is built by making decisions rather than by being kept away from them.
is-chatgpt-safe-for-kids:
Most services of this kind set a minimum age of thirteen, and some allow younger use with a parent's consent. Whether it is safe for your child is a different question from whether it is permitted, and it breaks into four risks that need different responses.

Risk one: it is confidently wrong

This is the most likely thing to actually happen and the least dramatic, which is why it is underrated. The system produces fluent, plausible statements that are false, with no signal distinguishing them from true ones. A child researching homework can absorb something incorrect and carry it for years.

What to do: show them. Ask it something you can verify and let them watch it be wrong. Establish the rule that anything factual gets checked somewhere else before it is used.

Risk two: content

The major services filter heavily and the filters mostly work. They are not perfect, they can be talked around by a determined teenager, and there are unfiltered alternatives a click away.

What to do: use it in a shared space for younger children, keep it on your account rather than theirs, and be specific that if something upsetting appears they should tell you and will not be in trouble.

Risk three: the relationship it invites

Less discussed and worth thinking about. These systems are agreeable, always available and never tired, which is precisely what makes them attractive to a lonely child. Companion-style apps go further deliberately.

A child confiding in something that cannot actually care, in place of a person who can, is a real thing and worth noticing.

What to do: pay attention to whether use is task-shaped or company-shaped. The first is fine; the second is worth a gentle conversation about what it is and is not.

Risk four: data

Conversations may be stored and may be used to improve the service. Children volunteer detail freely, including about other people.

What to do: turn off training on your conversations if the setting exists, and teach one rule: nothing you would not put on a noticeboard. No full names, no school, no address, nothing about a friend's private life.

What a reasonable setup looks like

Under about ten: only with you, on your account, for a specific purpose. Not a thing they open alone.

Ten to thirteen: shared account, shared space, particular tasks, conversations about what it got wrong.

Thirteen and up: their own use, with an agreed line on schoolwork, the checking habit established, and the data rule understood.

The honest summary

The realistic risk for most children is not something disturbing appearing on screen. It is a slow, invisible one: getting used to fluent answers without checking them, and doing less of their own thinking because something adequate is always available.

That risk is not addressed by settings. It is addressed by a habit of asking how do you know, applied often enough that the child applies it themselves.
should-kids-use-chatgpt-for-homework:
There is a line, and it is worth drawing it explicitly with your child rather than leaving them to guess, because the guessing is where the trouble comes from.

The principle

Homework exists to make a child practise something. Anything that increases the practice is fine. Anything that removes it defeats the purpose, however good the finished work looks.

Notice this has nothing to do with whether it counts as cheating. A child can stay within every school rule and still have skipped the thing the exercise was for.

Fine

  • Explaining a concept they did not follow in class, in a different way
  • Testing them on material they have revised
  • Checking a finished answer, after they have produced it
  • Explaining why their own working is wrong, once they have shown it
  • Giving them prompts to react to when they cannot start
  • Defining words in a text they are reading

Not fine

  • Writing any part of what is submitted
  • Producing the answer to the set question
  • Summarising a text they were meant to read
  • Doing the arithmetic they are learning to do
  • Translating a passage they were meant to translate
  • Generating ideas that are then handed in as their own thinking

The grey area, honestly

Structuring an essay. Improving sentences they wrote. Fixing their code after they have tried. These genuinely sit in between, and the answer depends on what is being assessed.

If the exercise is about structure, then getting structure from a machine skips it. If the exercise is about the history and the structure is incidental, it is closer to using a spellchecker.

Worth deciding case by case, out loud, with the child. The deciding is itself the useful part.

The one check that works

Explain it to me without the screen.

Make it routine rather than suspicious, and it does two jobs at once. It reveals whether the understanding is there, and it forces retrieval, which is one of the better-established ways of making something stick. A child who knows this happens tends to use the tool differently in the first place.

What to say to a child who is already doing it

Not an accusation. The more effective conversation is about the trade: you can hand in better work this term and know less at the end of it, and the bill arrives in an exam hall or the first time somebody asks you to do it unaided.

Most children find that argument reasonable, partly because it treats them as capable of weighing something rather than as caught.

And the part parents avoid

If homework is so dull, so long or so far beyond them that the only sane response is to shortcut it, that is worth knowing and worth raising with the school. Sometimes the tool is not the problem; it is the thing revealing one.
